paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend. Elihu looks at a storm and sees a God too great for anybody to figure out. He says, "God is great—beyond our knowledge" (Job 36:26), and then he points at rain, lightning and thunder to prove it. When you can't explain a cloud, you probably shouldn't be writing God's performance review.

Now, I want to be careful. Elihu says some true things, like "He is exalted in power!" and that God "does not oppress" (Job 37:23). But Elihu also tells Job that judgment has seized him because of wickedness (Job 36:17), and the text never says that Job's suffering is that kind of judgment. Elihu is a man with a lot of words, and I think he's sure of more than he can see. So the lesson isn't "suffering always means you did something." The lesson is that God is far bigger than our explanations for Him.

So here's what to bake into your heart today. Stand still, like Elihu says: "Listen to this, O Job; stand still and consider the wonders of God" (Job 37:14). When life makes no sense, you don't have to have the answer. You just have to know Who is in charge of the storm, and Elihu says even that storm comes "in His loving devotion" (Job 37:13). Job's story isn't over, friend, and neither is this one.
